concepts.title: Array scans and accumulators
concepts.competency: Use a scan when the answer can be updated from the current value and a small amount of earlier state.
concepts.explanation: Read the integer count before the values. Visit indices 0 through n-1 once. Choose an initial accumulator that matches the operation: zero for a sum or count; the first value for a minimum of a nonempty array. State what the accumulator means after each visited prefix. Handle n=0 explicitly when permitted.
examples: For [4, -2, 7], a running sum starts at 0 and becomes 4, 2, 9. After index 1, exactly the first two values have contributed.
misconceptions: Boundary conditions and absence must be checked explicitly.
concepts.accessibility: Plain text, zero-based indices, explicit input/output; no color or diagram required.

concepts.title: Search with explicit absence and position
concepts.competency: Use a linear scan when no ordering or searchable index has been promised.
concepts.explanation: Scan for a target using equality. For the first match, return immediately; for the last match, keep replacing the saved index. Use -1 for absence and keep indices zero-based. Repeated targets make first, last and count different questions. A nearest-value search instead tracks the smallest distance seen; update only for a strictly better distance to preserve the first position in a tie.
examples: In [6, 2, 6], target 6 first appears at index 0, last appears at index 2, and appears twice. Target 9 is absent.
misconceptions: Boundary conditions and absence must be checked explicitly.
concepts.accessibility: Plain text, zero-based indices, explicit input/output; no color or diagram required.

concepts.title: Frequencies preserve multiplicity
concepts.competency: Use keyed counts when repeated values and their multiplicities affect the answer.
concepts.explanation: Map each distinct integer to its occurrence count. A set answers membership, while a frequency map also records repeats. To count equal-value index pairs, each new occurrence pairs with all earlier occurrences of that value. For the first unique value, count first and then scan the original order.
examples: For [8, 8, -1, 8], frequencies are 8:3 and -1:1. The three occurrences of 8 yield three distinct index pairs; the first unique value has index 2.
misconceptions: Boundary conditions and absence must be checked explicitly.
concepts.accessibility: Plain text, zero-based indices, explicit input/output; no color or diagram required.

concepts.title: Prefix sums and boundaries
concepts.competency: Use prefix sums for repeated additive range queries or to compare left and right totals.
concepts.explanation: Define prefix[0]=0 and prefix[i+1]=prefix[i]+a[i]. Then the sum of the half-open range [l,r) is prefix[r]-prefix[l]. Negative values are allowed, so a running sum need not increase. Always decide whether a queried prefix must be nonempty.
examples: For [3, -5, 4], the prefix array is [0, 3, -2, 2]. The sum of [1,3) is prefix[3]-prefix[1]=2-3=-1.
misconceptions: Boundary conditions and absence must be checked explicitly.
concepts.accessibility: Plain text, zero-based indices, explicit input/output; no color or diagram required.

concepts.title: Two pointers with a reason to move
concepts.competency: Use opposing pointers with an ordering argument, or read/write pointers when retaining a stable compacted subsequence.
concepts.explanation: Two pointers must have distinct roles. In a sorted pair-sum search, use the leftmost and rightmost remaining values, moving left forward when the sum is too small and right backward when too large. In a palindrome check, compare symmetric positions. In sorted deduplication, a read pointer scans input and a write pointer bounds the unique output.
examples: Sorted [1, 3, 5, 9] with target 8: 1+9 is too large, then 1+5 too small, then 3+5 matches. These moves rely on sorted order.
misconceptions: Boundary conditions and absence must be checked explicitly.
concepts.accessibility: Plain text, zero-based indices, explicit input/output; no color or diagram required.

concepts.title: Fixed-size windows and outgoing values
concepts.competency: Use a fixed window when the size is specified and the aggregate supports removal and insertion.
concepts.explanation: For a window of k values, calculate the first aggregate once. Moving one position removes the outgoing contribution and adds the incoming contribution. Visit exactly n-k+1 windows. Initialize a maximum from the first window, not zero, because all sums can be negative. This fixed-window rule does not justify a variable-size sum search with negative values.
examples: For [4, -2, 7, 1] and k=2, window sums are 2, 5, 8. Move from 2 to 5 by subtracting 4 and adding 7.
misconceptions: Boundary conditions and absence must be checked explicitly.
concepts.accessibility: Plain text, zero-based indices, explicit input/output; no color or diagram required.

lessons.title: Search with explicit absence and position
lessons.instruction: Check the constraints and edge cases, estimate complexity, then attempt independently. Timing is low-stakes practice. Scan for a target using equality. For the first match, return immediately; for the last match, keep replacing the saved index. Use -1 for absence and keep indices zero-based. Repeated targets make first, last and count different questions. A nearest-value search instead tracks the smallest distance seen; update only for a strictly better distance to preserve the first position in a tie.
examples: In [6, 2, 6], target 6 first appears at index 0, last appears at index 2, and appears twice. Target 9 is absent.
lessons.language_notes: Use vector<long long> for values and long long for sums. Cast sizes deliberately when using signed pointer indices; unsigned n-1 underflows for an empty vector. Compile as C++20.
lessons.pattern_recognition: Use a linear scan when no ordering or searchable index has been promised.
lessons.correctness: All positions before the current index have been examined. A first match cannot have an earlier unexamined match; a saved last match is replaced only by a later equal value.
lessons.complexity: Worst-case O(n) time, O(1) auxiliary space. An early return improves some inputs without changing the worst case.

lessons.title: Frequencies preserve multiplicity
lessons.instruction: Dry-run the example before coding. Write down the state after every step. Map each distinct integer to its occurrence count. A set answers membership, while a frequency map also records repeats. To count equal-value index pairs, each new occurrence pairs with all earlier occurrences of that value. For the first unique value, count first and then scan the original order.
examples: For [8, 8, -1, 8], frequencies are 8:3 and -1:1. The three occurrences of 8 yield three distinct index pairs; the first unique value has index 2.
lessons.language_notes: Use zero-based list indices and range(n). Python integers handle these sums. Avoid a mutable default argument; negative indices access from the end and are not an absence sentinel.
lessons.pattern_recognition: Use keyed counts when repeated values and their multiplicities affect the answer.
lessons.correctness: After each update, each stored count equals occurrences of its key in the visited prefix. Every equal pair is counted exactly when its later endpoint is visited.
lessons.complexity: With hash maps, expected O(n) time and O(d) auxiliary space for d distinct values; hash operations do not promise worst-case constant time.

lessons.title: Prefix sums and boundaries
lessons.instruction: Dry-run the example before coding. Write down the state after every step. Define prefix[0]=0 and prefix[i+1]=prefix[i]+a[i]. Then the sum of the half-open range [l,r) is prefix[r]-prefix[l]. Negative values are allowed, so a running sum need not increase. Always decide whether a queried prefix must be nonempty.
examples: For [3, -5, 4], the prefix array is [0, 3, -2, 2]. The sum of [1,3) is prefix[3]-prefix[1]=2-3=-1.
lessons.language_notes: Use zero-based list indices and range(n). Python integers handle these sums. Avoid a mutable default argument; negative indices access from the end and are not an absence sentinel.
lessons.pattern_recognition: Use prefix sums for repeated additive range queries or to compare left and right totals.
lessons.correctness: Induction on i establishes that prefix[i] equals the sum of exactly the first i elements. Subtraction removes the shared initial prefix.
lessons.complexity: O(n) preprocessing and storage; each range-sum query is O(1). A running-prefix search can use O(1) auxiliary space.

lessons.title: Fixed-size windows and outgoing values
lessons.instruction: Dry-run the example before coding. Write down the state after every step. For a window of k values, calculate the first aggregate once. Moving one position removes the outgoing contribution and adds the incoming contribution. Visit exactly n-k+1 windows. Initialize a maximum from the first window, not zero, because all sums can be negative. This fixed-window rule does not justify a variable-size sum search with negative values.
examples: For [4, -2, 7, 1] and k=2, window sums are 2, 5, 8. Move from 2 to 5 by subtracting 4 and adding 7.
lessons.language_notes: Use zero-based list indices and range(n). Python integers handle these sums. Avoid a mutable default argument; negative indices access from the end and are not an absence sentinel.
lessons.pattern_recognition: Use a fixed window when the size is specified and the aggregate supports removal and insertion.
lessons.correctness: After each move the saved sum equals exactly the current k elements, since one departing value is subtracted and the new value is added. Every legal start is processed once.
lessons.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary state for sum/count aggregates. Per-window output occupies O(n-k+1).

exit_check.prompt: Give the maximum size-2 window sum in [-4, -2, -7].
